name: Desiccated thyroid (Armour)

lead: Desiccated thyroid is dried animal thyroid gland that supplies both T4 and T3 hormone. People who talk about it for looks are after a faster metabolism, lower body fat and a leaner look. Armour Thyroid is the best-known brand.

The chain runs through thyroid hormone receptors: added T4 and T3 raise metabolic rate, which in theory means more energy burned. It is an older hypothyroidism treatment, and excessive thyroid hormone does cause weight loss in medical settings, but no study has tested it as a slimming treatment in people with normal thyroid function.

paras: It is a prescription treatment for an underactive thyroid, taken by mouth. Some people with normal thyroid function discuss adding it to a diet and training plan to support fat loss. Medical use is monitored with blood tests, and guidelines generally prefer synthetic levothyroxine for hypothyroidism.

Excess thyroid hormone can cause fast or irregular heartbeat, anxiety, fever and, at worst, heart failure. Batch variability and high T3 peaks are cited concerns. It is prescription-only and is not indicated for weight loss.

angle.text: Desiccated thyroid supplies T4 and T3, and people use it hoping the extra hormone raises metabolic rate and helps them carry less body fat. It is an older hypothyroidism treatment; no trials have tested it for slimming.

lead: Desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) is dried, powdered thyroid gland, usually from pigs, taken by mouth as a prescription treatment for hypothyroidism. Armour Thyroid is the best-known brand [1]. Because thyroid hormone sets the body's metabolic rate, people with an underactive thyroid can experience weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance and dry skin and hair, and the aim of treatment is to restore normal thyroid function [2]. The appearance link is therefore a chain: thyroid hormone replacement -> normalised metabolism and energy -> easing of the weight, skin and hair changes that accompany hypothyroidism. Some patients and prescribers prefer DTE to synthetic levothyroxine, and in some wellness and bodybuilding settings it is also discussed as a way to raise metabolic rate and manage weight [1].

The extract contains both thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), in a ratio of roughly 4:1, compared with about 11:1 in humans; one grain (64.8 mg) is reported to contain about 38 micrograms of T4 and 9 of T3 [1]. It was the main hypothyroidism treatment from the 1890s until synthetic levothyroxine replaced it from the 1960s [1][3]. The American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the Royal College of Physicians recommend levothyroxine over thyroid extract, and the American Thyroid Association names levothyroxine as the preferred treatment [1].

Randomized trials in hypothyroid patients have compared DTE with levothyroxine and with levothyroxine plus liothyronine. In one 70-patient crossover study, participants lost about 3 lb on DTE, and just under half preferred it [4]. Excess thyroid hormone doses can cause weight loss but also fever, anxiety, arrhythmias and heart failure [1]. No studies have tested DTE as a slimming treatment in people with normal thyroid function.
infobox: Natural thyroid, pork thyroid, thyroid USP, thyroid BP [1]

paras: DTE is used for hypothyroidism, the deficiency of thyroid hormone. The most common cause is chronic autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's), and classic symptoms include fatigue, lethargy, weight gain and cold intolerance [2]. Levothyroxine monotherapy is the standard of care and restores thyroid function tests to the reference range in most patients [2]. A minority of patients remain symptomatic on levothyroxine and report better outcomes with a combination containing liothyronine or with DTE [5].

Arguments made in favour of DTE include that it supplies T3 as well as T4 and that some patients prefer it. Arguments against include batch variability, supraphysiologic T3 peaks and the risk of symptom-based high dosing; guideline bodies cite the lack of long-term randomized safety data [1]. Maximal effects of a dose can take up to three weeks, and regular blood tests are recommended to check that the dose is appropriate [1]. In the United States it ranked about 141st among prescribed medicines in 2023, with more than 3 million prescriptions [1].

Weight change is one of the most visible effects of thyroid hormone status, and hypothyroid symptoms can include weight gain and dry or thin hair and skin [2]. For patients with a diagnosed deficiency, treatment aims to return these features toward baseline as thyroid function normalises.

Outside medical settings, DTE is sometimes discussed for weight management and leaner body composition; reference sources note that excessive doses can cause weight loss along with fever, anxiety, arrhythmias and heart failure [1]. For the related synthetic T3 drug liothyronine, the US label carries a boxed warning stating that, in people with normal thyroid function, doses within the range of daily hormonal requirements are ineffective for weight reduction, and that larger doses can cause serious or life-threatening toxicity [6]. No clinical trial has tested DTE for cosmetic weight loss in people with normal thyroid function.

DTE contains a mixture of T4 and T3 from the animal gland, with a T4:T3 ratio of about 4:1 compared with about 11:1 in humans [1]. Pork is the usual source today; potency was once specified only by iodine content [1]. T3 is the more potent thyroid hormone: it raises basal metabolic rate and acts faster and for a shorter time than T4 [6]. Proponents of DTE argue that the extract contains the full range of thyroid hormones, while reference sources note that the body normally regulates T3 production from T4 itself, one reason for the move to levothyroxine [1].

Brands differ in manufacturer and fillers, and the same hormone content is expressed in grains rather than micrograms [1]. A 1980 JAMA investigation found large variation in hormone content between American products, a historical concern that remains part of the debate over whether to prescribe DTE [1].

A 2024 Lancet review states that levothyroxine monotherapy is safe, inexpensive and improves symptoms in most patients [2]. A review of quality of life in hypothyroidism concluded that neither levothyroxine plus liothyronine studies nor DTE had shown robust improvements in patient satisfaction [7].

In a network meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials (8 crossover) with 1,135 patients, 52% of patients preferred levothyroxine plus liothyronine or DTE, 24% preferred levothyroxine alone and 24% had no preference; the relative risk for preferring combination therapy was 2.20 [5]. An online survey of hypothyroid patients reported prominent dissatisfaction with levothyroxine therapy, with about 15% more levothyroxine users reporting impaired quality of life than controls [8].

Thyroid extract was the earliest oral treatment for hypothyroidism. George Redmayne Murray described treating myxedema with it in 1891, and reported a 28-year successful treatment in 1920 [1]. Armour and Company supplied the best-known brand, and Westhroid became a commercial option in 1934 [1]. Use declined from the early 1960s as synthetic levothyroxine offered consistent potency; by the 1980s more patients received synthetic T4 or T4/T3 combinations than extract [1][3]. Reasons cited for the shift include variable hormone content, supraphysiologic T3 levels and the view that the body makes its own T3 [1].

A 2016 Annals of Internal Medicine history of hypothyroid treatment traces the move from extracts to synthetic hormones and the continuing interest in combination therapy [3]. Prescriptions have fallen since the 1960s but remain substantial, at more than 3 million a year in the United States [1].

Excess doses may cause weight loss, fever, headache, anxiety, insomnia, arrhythmias and heart failure; allergic reactions are possible [1]. Dosing by symptoms rather than by laboratory results often leads to higher doses, and higher doses carry a risk of worsening osteoporosis; hyperthyroidism is linked to poorer bone density and more atrial fibrillation in older patients [1]. In the 2021 crossover trial, DTE produced a minor increase in heart rate [9]. Regular blood tests are recommended [1]. Use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is described as generally safe [1].

A randomized, double-blind crossover study of 70 adults with primary hypothyroidism on stable levothyroxine compared DTE and levothyroxine for 16 weeks each. Symptoms and neurocognitive measures did not differ; patients lost about 3 lb on DTE (172.9 versus 175.7 lb), and 48.6% preferred DTE, 18.6% preferred levothyroxine and 32.9% had no preference [4].

A 2021 prospective randomized, double-blind crossover study of 75 hypothyroid patients compared levothyroxine, levothyroxine plus liothyronine and DTE for 22 weeks; serum TSH stayed in range in all arms, and primary outcomes did not differ except a minor heart-rate increase on DTE [9].

Registered trials include a completed phase 2 study of Armour Thyroid versus levothyroxine in previously hypothyroid participants (NCT04124705, n=284) [10], an older randomized study comparing DTE and levothyroxine (NCT01739972, n=180) [11] and a recruiting phase 3 single-arm study of a porcine thyroid extract tablet (NCT07747103, n=466) [12]. No studies found of DTE for cosmetic weight loss.

DTE is sold under prescription-only status in the United States and is listed on DailyMed [1]. Several brands exist, including Armour Thyroid, NP Thyroid and Nature-Throid, as well as the generic names natural thyroid, pork thyroid and thyroid USP [1]. Patient communities and some clinicians favour it for patients who feel unwell on levothyroxine, while professional societies recommend levothyroxine first [1][5].

The patient-dissatisfaction survey published in Thyroid in 2018 is often cited in discussions of why some people seek alternatives to levothyroxine [8]. Professional guidance from the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the Royal College of Physicians recommends levothyroxine in preference to thyroid extract, citing superphysiologic T3 levels and the absence of long-term randomized safety data [1].

lore.intro: In wellness, metabolism-focused and bodybuilding settings, DTE is discussed both as a hypothyroidism option and as a way to raise metabolic rate for leaner body composition [1]. The claims below describe what proponents say and what clinical sources report.

claims.claim: Because it contains T3 as well as T4, desiccated thyroid is more complete than levothyroxine.
Many patients feel better on desiccated thyroid than on levothyroxine.
Desiccated thyroid can raise metabolism enough to help people lose fat even when thyroid tests are normal.
Dosing by symptoms rather than by blood tests suits people who feel unwell with normal results.
Treating an underactive thyroid improves weight, skin and hair.
